title: Kepler Defends His Mother Against Witchcraft
text:
In 1615, in the small town of Leonberg in Wurttemberg, a neighbor named Ursula Reinbold accused Katharina Kepler, a widow of about seventy, of poisoning her with a potion. Katharina was known as a sharp-tongued woman who made herbal remedies. Accusations multiplied, and she was formally charged with witchcraft. In that region and era, such charges could end in torture and burning.

Her son was Johannes Kepler, imperial mathematician, the astronomer who had discovered that the planets move in ellipses. He was then living in Linz, in Austria, working on his astronomy. He put much of it aside to defend her. He studied the law, wrote long legal arguments refuting each accusation, and traveled to Wurttemberg to be at her side.

In August 1620 Katharina was arrested and held in chains for about fourteen months. In September 1621 the court ordered her to be taken to the torture chamber, shown the instruments and threatened with their use, in the hope that she would confess. She refused, saying they could do what they liked but she had nothing to confess. In October 1621, thanks largely to her son's defense, she was released.

Katharina died about six months later. Kepler returned to his work and in 1627 published the Rudolphine Tables, the most accurate planetary tables of his time.
lesson: Some causes are worth more than our career, and a parent in danger is one of them. Standing by family when the whole town turns against them takes real courage.
people: Johannes Kepler, Katharina Kepler, Ursula Reinbold
source: Trial records (Kepler's defense briefs); Ulinka Rublack, The Astronomer and the Witch (2015)
